newsitem.title: UK: Bank of England denies its star is waning.
newsitem.headline: Bank of England denies its star is waning.

text.p: The head of The Bank of England, Britain's central bank, denied on Wednesday it was being stripped of power by the new Labour government and promised the BoE would remain active well into the next century.
BoE Governor Eddie George said he already worked a 26-hour day and had no desire to increase his workload, putting a decidely brave face on the latest government move to modernise Britain's economy.
On Tuesday, finance minister Gordon Brown announced plans to transfer supervision of Britain's thriving finanical services sector to a new beefed-up Securities and Investment Board (SIB).
Currently, the BoE is in charge of regulating banks but it has presided over a series of embarrassing scandals in recent years and faced accusations of sleeping on the job.
In today's interlocking industry, Brown said the unwieldy system whereby the BoE watches over banks while a raft of lesser bodies supervise related industries was ripe for overhaul.

The new all-in-one regulator would be in charge of banks, securites firms and insurance companies, making it one of the most powerful bodies in Britain but leaving the BoE stripped of one of its core jobs.
George insisted the move made "entirely good sense" and was "sensible in its own terms" even if he himself would not have backed such a change just now.
"You can skin a cat in all sorts of different ways and they all have pros and cons," he said in a determined, if lukewarm, show of support.
But he did admit the surprise move had prompted thoughts of resignation and pointedly said the government had told him about its plan, not consulted him.
"All sorts of thoughts go through your mind," he said wistfully. "I didn't seriously think about resigning."

The move came two weeks after Brown gave the BoE unprecedented power to set interest rates -- a move widely applauded by the City -- but said the 300-year-old central bank would no longer oversee the gilt market and auctions of government debt.
George insisted he was not fazed by the changes, saying few other central banks had enjoyed his wide-ranging powers, and dismissed talk of a fiscal strip tease being forced upon the Bank.

He said the Bank -- which by tradition spars with government over the levers of economic power -- looked forward to a "period of change and development" under the new Labour government, swept to power this month after 18 years in opposition.

Indeed, George laughed off suggestions the BoE's last remaining major powers would vanish if and when Britain joined a single European currency, when national central bank functions would transfer to a European Union bank.
But wasn't a slow strip tease already underway, reporters asked, whereby the august central bank would end up dancing down Threadneedle Street in its underwear?
"I don't think you need worry. We will still be here in 10 years," George said. "I think we will still be quite well clothed in 10 years time too."
